coachingPoints: Scout tendencies, not just plays — what a team does under pressure matters most.
Update the report after the first matchup; teams evolve across a season.
Share only what is actionable with players; keep the full report for the staff.
Always scout yourself too — know what opponents see when they watch you.
commonMistakes: Scouting only one game and preparing for an outlier performance.
Handing players a ten-page report they will never read.
Focusing on the opponent so much that you forget your own strengths.
Not adjusting the scout when the game starts differently than expected.
description: A practical scouting system — what to watch, how to organize it, and how to turn observations into a winning game plan.
gameSituations: Preparing for a playoff series against a familiar rival.
Tournament play with one day to scout a completely unknown team.
Mid-season rematch: adjusting the scout based on the first meeting.

howTo.detail: One game is a highlight reel of lies — shooting luck and matchups distort everything. Patterns in personnel and actions only emerge across multiple games.
howTo.title: Watch two to three full games

howTo.detail: For each rotation player, note strengths, weaknesses, shooting spots, and defensive liabilities. Personnel wins and loses games more than plays do.
howTo.title: Chart personnel

howTo.detail: Find the sets and actions they run most often and diagram them for your team. If you can defend their top three actions, you can defend them.
howTo.title: Identify their top three actions

howTo.detail: Poor transition defense? Weak closeouts? A star who never helps? Every team has soft spots — find them and build your attack around them.
howTo.title: Find the vulnerabilities

howTo.detail: Personnel notes, keys to the game, and specific matchups on a single page. If it does not fit on one page, it is too long to use.
howTo.title: Write the one-page report

howTo.detail: Have your scout team run the opponent's actions in practice so your defense gets live reps against them before game day. Recognition comes from repetition.
howTo.title: Translate it to practice

title: Scouting Opponents
whatIsIt: Scouting is the systematic study of an opponent: their personnel, tendencies, favorite actions, and weaknesses. Done well, it turns the unknown into the familiar — your players recognize the opponent's favorite play because they have already defended it in practice.

Effective scouting is selective. You cannot prepare for everything, so you prepare for what matters most: who takes the big shots, what they run in late-clock situations, and where they are vulnerable.
whyItMatters: Scouting wins games before they start. Knowing that their point guard always drives left, or that they never defend the skip pass, gives your team concrete edges. At higher levels everyone scouts — the advantage goes to whoever translates scouting into the clearest plan.
It also builds player confidence. Athletes who have seen the opponent's actions on film and defended them in practice walk onto the court believing they are ready — because they are.
